But this protest is not sufficient ; if it is to I effect any good, it must be carried into the Council itself with a petition for an investigation and a decision tending to unseat the members thus elected. Even if crowned with no result, this step of itself will teach the guilty | parties a salutary lesson, aud it will open their eyes to the fact they seem to ignore, that their ; usurpation of the franchise may be resisted, and that the citizens of this Island will not tolerate their rights to bo wrested from them and made a mockery of, or may ho, turned against them, by a few individuals so circumstanced as to possess that power, and so unscrupulous as to exercise it. Therefore, a petition should be filed and proofs collected, to be laid before the Colonial-Council immediately on its opening, showing how voters wire ordered to voto for the elected members, and how iu consequence, the elections must be held to be null and void. If the eitizeus care for their rights they would take that step and not be scared from it by a little inconvenience. A public meeting eouj venod for that purposo and appointing a committee of acting, wsuld of course he the best j method to be used for the purpose, aud the i meeting would undoubtedly express the public sense of the outrage committed upon the public at the last election. We would thus openly and publicly, in the most practical and wholesome manner expose the secret intrigues of some people, who deem themselves above our reach,

1 and who seem to think, that il they arc good enough to elect themselves our Councilmcn, we should bow down to them for serving us so. The latest accounts from Copenhagen inform 1 us, that there is every probability that the sessions of the Colonial-Council will hereafter he held publicly. Should this take place at the now approaching session of the Council, þÿ and I see no reason why his Excellency the Governor should not as to so desirable a measure anticipate the almost certain vote of the Diet, and at once declare the sessions open to the public, þÿ should this take place, 1 say, then such a petition will be sure of effecting a useful result, as the debates upon it will he held before the public, and wo would obtain a fair treatment, if not from a sense of justice, at least from a cling of shame in the members. But, whether the ne xt session be public, or not, certain it is, that if people want their rights, they must themselves staud up and defend them, and if they let others deprive them of these rights without resistance, then they deserve to lose them.

ST. THOMAS. To the Editor of the þÿ St. Thomce þÿTidende Sib, þÿ In your paper of the 19th inst. you have inserted an article by Lawyer IIeilbuth, taken from the St. Croix Avis, wherein lie asserts that the election for members to the Colonial Council, which took place on the 8th inst., must be regarded as invalid in consequence of presumed informalities, pointed out by him. As we are of the opinion that he is mistaken in the view he has taken of the matter, we would solicit a space in your paper for the following remarks : þÿ In as far as Mr. IIhilbuth finds cause to regret that the day fixed by Government for the election was a Saturday7, i whereby the Israelites were prevented from voting, it can certainly not be denied that it would have been desirable if Government from such motive had appointed another day ; but, that the result of the election would for that reason have been quite different, there exists | not the slightest probability, as the Israelites of this plaee have no interest in connection with the election, distinct from that of their fellow citizens, a fact which has been evidenced by preceding elections. We are not aware either of any exceptions having been made against the day fixed lor the election which was published ten days previous. Nor can we for one moment entertain the idea, which the article in question seems to imply, that our Israelitish fellow citizens would on this occasion have united contrary to what they have before manifested, to carry out an election in opposition to what experience has shown to be the opinion of tho

public large. at The rectitude and independence of character (it is with pleasure we record it) which distinguish them, would deter them from entertaining any such measures, even should there be persons canvassing for votes in that direction, and should Government, for other motives, direct another election to take place, we are convinced that the result will show we are not mistaken in our opinion of our respectable mosaic fellow citizens. With regard to the opinion expressed by Mr. Heilbuth, that the election must bo looked upon as null and void from the circumstance of the Director of the Poll and his Assistants not having voted, we cannot refrain Irom utte'ing our surprise that he, whose piofession it is to expound the law, should advance such an averuieut. The 18th of the Colonial Law referred to, prescribes when the Committee of Election are to poll their votes, but contains no injunction that they shall vote ; for such an injunction would undoubtedly be an absurdity, as the voting for Members to the Colonial Council is a voluntary, and not a compulsory act for all and every one qualified thereto ; it can therefore not be supposed that the far from pleasing task of sitting for four hours in such a Committee, to attend to the election, should deprive them of the rights to abstain from voting. To the contrary we opine that, in exercising this right, the Public is indebted to the Comtniit< e lor the tact shown in not voting, as their votes cuu d have given another colour to the result of the election
than that which it ought to have, by the fact of one solitary individual only having record' d his vote. I am, Mr. Editor. Your obdt. servant.

If the dispatch is ever published, it will produce a sensation, especially in the slave-buying States.

Mr. Douglas declares that mote Africans have been imported into the United States during the last year than duriug any year when the traffic was legal. Wc presume that this is perfectly true ; at any rate, wo must believe that Mr. Douglas bas ample means of knowing whereof he affirms. After months of neglect, during which the trade bas become established, and after the energetic remonstrance of h-.rd John Russell, the Administration are taking measures to check it. Eight vessels are ordered to the coast of Africa ; the naval depot there has been removed much nearer to the slave-buying region ; and four steamers arc ordered to cruise in the Gulf of Mexico to previ nt the landing of cargoes either in Cuba or the United States." We shall watch with interest, the proceedings of these squadrons. But it is not likely that they will accomplish anything of much importance. The slavers will avoid them ; or il they are arrested, they will be tried before Southern Jury and Southern Judges, by whom they will be acquitted.

FRIDAY, 4tii NOVEMBER, 1859. þÿ þÿ The R. M. Steam Packet Shannon arrived at Si. Thomas on the 1st inst. The affairs of Italy become daily more complica'ed. The great Powers have agreed to meet in Congress, together with Sardinia, Sweden, Spain, Portugal, Naples and Rome. The deliberations at Zurich seem t<> have arrived at a dead stop, respecting the amount of the Lombard debt; although conflicting re|>orts are circulated to the effect, that all the other stipulations have been agreed on. Early in life he had entered into the army ot Maria Louisa, and soon became known to the people of Parma for his hatred to the Liberal party of the Duchy. At the accession of the late Duke of Lucca he was still a captain, but, having discharged with great eagerness all the missions which were entrusted to him when the Italian patriots were to be persecuted, he rapidly rose to the ranks of Colonel and Chamberlain, and was made a Knight of three different Orders. At the restoration of Charles III., Colonel Anviti became the intimate friend of the youiig Duke, aud the ag. nt of those deeds which brought the first-named Prince to his blood-stained grave. FRANCE. on The Tuesday: Paris þÿ correspondent þÿ I have received of the Times writes a piece of intelligence of so singular and important a uatu.i that I should hesitate to communicate it to v u (or publication had I not gic.it confidence in tin opportunities aud veracity of my informant. It is to the effect that tho French Government, pioposes to claim from Piedmont the expense it incurred in the late war with Austria. We are somewhat accustomed to unexpected and startling acts on the part of the present Government of France, and also to hear strange tiling- pro dicutcd as likely to be done by it; we have beard people talk of an invasion of England, of a march upon the Rhine, of tlie establishment of French imperial scions iu Italian kingdoms þÿ of a host of things, in short, more or less probable or improbable, but to me, at least, it lias not occurred to hear anybody suggest tlie probability of France demanding fron: Piedmont payment for her late 8. rviccs to Italy. Such, however, 1 have strong reason to believe, is the þÿEmperor s intention ; and, perhaps, if we do not confine ourselves too strictly to tlie bare fact, but look at the matter from another point of view, we may find tlie project neatly identical with one that was long attributed to him. Notwithstanding her recent acquisition of a rich province, Piedmont is in no position to meet the various heavy pecuniary claims made upon her. In tho first place, Austria demands from her late antagonist 400,000,000 francs, and, although

this is likely to be ultimately much reduced þÿ probably to 250,000 000, or thereabouts þÿ it will still be a severe pull on Sardinian resources. France claims a handsome sum as ind mniiy lor the unpaid pensious charged on the Lombardo- Venetian Monte iund, for the benefit of certain dignitaries of the First Empire þÿ pension- which have not been paid since 1815. A portion of this sum is claimed from Austria; the remaining and larger part is to lull on Piedmont, who seems expected to pay on all sides, to allies as well as to enemies Now, it is no news to anybody punishment in the presence of the Colonel, who I that the Piedmontese finances are in anything

but a flourishing condition; tint the revenue has there long been exceeded by the expenditure, that frequent loans have been contracted, and that the late war has occasioned a further great increase in the burdens of the Treasury. Lombardy, certainly a rich addition to the dominions of the House of Savoy, has burdens of her own, and, moreover, her provinces are by no means in a uniformly flourishing state, nearly all of them having suffered for some years past from the vine disease and the degeneracy of the silkworm, much more than from the Austrian misrule, to which the Lombards were fond of attributing all their ills and hisses, while some, the Valtelline for instance, have been completely impoverished and ruined by the same causes. The demands of Austria are not on y resisted by Sardinia, but do not receive the support of France, who has proposed to Austria and Piedmont to submit the disputed point to the arbitration of another Power. A Paris letter in the Nord says: þÿ 1 learn that the signing of the treaty of peace at Zurich may be look, d on as decidedly adjourned lor the moment, in consequence of difficulties raised by Austria, and which could not be removed by Prince de Metternich at Biarritz. The last conversation of the Austrian Ambassador with the Emperor took place in the presence of the Prince of Oldenburg and of Lord Cowley. Prince Metternich developed at length the reasons for which Austria insisted on the necessity of reproducing in the treaty of peace the p ,, liminaries ol Vtllafranca ns r girds the recall of the Archdukes; it was true, he said, that the Emperor Francis Joseph had undertaken not to employ force to re-establish the dispossessed members of his family, but the principle that they should lie recalled was not stipulated at Vilhtfranca without good reasons, and it ought therefore, to be maintained and respected in tbo definitive treaty of peace. of the Archdukes ns to constitute a fait accompli which both jusiicc and the most vulgar prudence required to be taken into account. Annexation, he added, was an act of another kind, and Europe would be free in a Congress to accept or lvjcot it, without exciting latal conflicts. Prince do Metternich added that he profoundly regretted the incideut, which would adjourn the renewal of amicable relations between France and Austria The Emperor begged the Austrian diplomatist to communicate to the Emperor Francis Joseph the grave motives which, under present circumstances, should induce him not to seek the sense of the bnscs of Villafranca by exaggerating them. Carl Hattensen, const. COMMUNICATION. The Aurora of 29th August last (1859.) To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis This Aurora which extended over the whole of Europe, over the Atlantic reaching Bermuda, Cuba and Jamaica, has extended over Australia in the Southern Hemisphere, where on the 29th August, it rendered for a time all communication between the cities of Sydney, Melbourne, and Adelaide by the electric Telegraph impracticable, from its effect upon the wires By last Mail 1 have received from Melbourne a most particular and interesting description of its appearance, and extraordinary disturbance produced on the Magnetic Declination (variation of the Compass) and Intensity, but it is too long for insertion in your paper at present. It would appear that the whole atmosphere surrounding the Earth must have been more or less affected by it at the same moment of time. AM) LANG. St. Croix, 8th December 1859.

From the London Times. We cannot doubt that our readers have perused with much interest, and that interest by 110 means of uu agreeable kind, the account which we published ou Saturday last of the statements nnd arguments in the Revue liulepcndante, a French periodical published in London, conducted with much literary ability, and with as complete a knowledge as any one not connected with Government can have of the preseut state of affairs in France. We have no doubt that the facts which it states arc true, though we do not feel ourselves called upon to adopt implicitly the conclusions to which they lead. We must not forget that the wi iters of this periodical would rejoice in nothing; so much as in the overthrow of the present state of things in France, and we must be very careful not to allow ourselves to he carried away by their eloquence and t heir ahiliiy beyond the point to which calm aud dispassionate reason would lead us Rightly to appreciate the existing state of things on the other side of the British Channel is a problem of enormous þÿ of overwhelming, importance. Wc know no family having any claim to the throne of France from which wo have anything to expect which should render us desirous ot a new dynastic involution, and we are only too anxious to believe, it that belief can by any means ho maintained, that the Emperor Napoleon entertains towards this country those sentiments of amity and goodwill which he has so earnestly and repeatedly professed. We think it cannot be denied that, without,

so far as we are aware, the slightest provocation on the part of England, there exists in France at this moment a very strong and very wide-spread hostility to the Government and people of this country. We do nut lay particular stress on any oue conversation, either at a military festival when the tongue is loosed by wine, or iu a railway carriage, where the speakers are unkuown to each other ; but from information derived from a vast number of iudepcudutit sources we entertain no doubt that a feeling of hostility more bitter than has existed iu France since the peace of 1M5 is at this moment entertaiued towards this country The French Press, so guarded on all other subjects, is on this outspoken. The moderate and reasonable Journal des Debuts contains attacks up in England sucli as never before, in moiucuts of the greatest irritation, have appeared in its decorous columns. The (iazetle de France larks language to express tho biiteruess of its detestation, and the Univers is still more viiulent than the organ of the Legitimists. The talk of the Army and Navy is of revenge for victories 4 > nnd 55 years old, and their firm belief, as well as their ardent wish, is that in a few months the signal will be given for the invasion of this country. The inhabitants of the departments from Brest to Calais experience a revival of the hostility of 50 yenis since, and, strange to say, burn with ardour for a war of which they must bear the brunt. Wc believe this to be a fair representation of the present

state of feeling in France þÿ nay, mure, we believe the Emperor Napoleon himself would, if the iuestion could he put to him, admit it to he so. We believe he would tell us that he is our only friend, and that to his intervention alone we owo it that the two most powerful States of the world are not already involved in an exterminating conflict. File fact we þÿstate namely, that England is hated, and a war with her earnestly desired by the clergy, the Legitimists, the Army, and the inhabitants of the Northern provinces of France þÿ we think we may assume as perfectly well proved, and we do not expect that any of the journals of France will be bold eDough to deny it. The next question is, how does it happen, after a peace of 45 years, that this should be tho feeling of France towards us? To what cause are wo to attribute it? What provocation have wo given? What offensive claims have we put forward What have wo done in the last ten

years to make the France of 1859 more (hostile to us than the France of ten years ago ? We have fought aud bled together without, as far as we are aware, the slightest imputation on the good faith or honour of either nation. We are even now preparing a joint expedition, and, so far as we are aware, there is no part of the globe in which our interests come iu direct and hostile contact. We are utterly unconscious of having put forward any claims or entered upon any negotiations which even the £most perverse ingenuity can construe as hostile to French iuterests. The French subjects whom the fortune of war lias placed under our Government are admitted precisely to the same rights and privileges as our own people, and, as far as hospitality goes, it has been our honour and our pleasure to receive the representatives of every dynasty that has occupied the throne of Franco since the Revolution. There remain, certainly, the injuries given and reccivedduring the wars of the Revolution and of Napoleon; but they in no degree account for the phenomenon which wo are examining, þÿ the great inerease of French auimosity against England at the present moment, and a wish and expectation in a time of what ought to be profound peace of au almost immediate descent upon our shores. We fear that the fact which is unfortunately' so notorious cau be accounted for iu no other way than by the assumption that these evil passions have received a powerful impulse ! from the.J French Government itself. The time is come when it

is most friendly and most wise to speak plainly aud openly. In England the manifestation of a fct ling in different aud remote parts of the country is very easily accounted for. By the agency of railways and electric telegraphs all the information that can be procured on any subject of public interest is simultaneously laid before tho nation in the sheets of a free Press, and it is not marvellous if from the same facts pcopleshould arrive for themselves at the same conclusions. In France there are but two ways iu which the whole body of the nation can bo acted upon. The one is by the Press, and tho other by the actiou of the centralized authority, civil and military. The French Press is not exposed to censure, but the power of punishing a newspaper in France is so summary, so complete, and so irresistible, that tho director of the journal is forced to perform the office of censor himself, under pain of the immediate aud total confiscation of the valuable property committed to his charge. II he violates the law, þÿ and nothing is easier than to do so without the slightest moral or political guilt, þÿ he is liable to punishments of every degree of severity ; and, if he does not violate the laW, he may be warned, or bis journal suppressed without warning, at the pleasure of the Government. Not only must he insert nothin" which the Government disapproves; he is bound to insert any article which the Government may transmit to him as if it had emanated from himself a fact which has been made laughubly þÿ

manifest by the appearance of file same .sentiments, expressed in the same words, in the most remote parts of the country at the same time. It is not, therefore, too much to -ay that for so much of the present irritation of feeling as arises from the attacks of the Press upon England tho Government of France is responsible. To check them would require no exercise of power. Au intimation that they are displeasing to the (.iu vernment would have sufficed, and that intima tion has never been given. The other way by which the opinion of France may bo simultaneously moved is through tho official hieararcliy. The Minister of the Interior in Paris wields a power more tremendous than was ever vested iu any Minister of any Government. He lias but to express a wish, aud an enormous bureaucracy, whose ramifications extend to the smallest commune in Frauce, is immediately set in motion. Their advancement depends on their diligence ; their power penetrates everywhere, and their influence reaches every one. The same is the ease in the Army. The Minister of War has only to give the word, aud thousands of zealous emissaries are ready to propagate it like lightning through the ranks of 600,000 men. Has this influence been used in tho present instanoo to excite the feelings of citizen and soldier against England? Wo believe it has, and we believe it for three reasons. First, we believe it because

it is quite clear tbat an instrument less secret, and in the present state of society in France le.-s efficient, þÿ the Press, þÿ has been employed for this purpose. We believe it, secondly, because the results are such as an action of the Govern- I ment upon the people would be likely to produce ; and we believe it, thirdly, because we have observed in the open acts of the Government of France symptoms that it does not shrink from stimulating ill-will against this country. We will mention two instances þÿ first, the issuing the medal of St. Hel ena, and, secondly, the erectiou at the public expense of a monument, to oommemorate a repulse sustained by the English on the coast of Britanuy a hundred years ago. We have therefore, we think, established that there is considerable irritation in the mind ot the French Army and nation against England, and that that irritation has mainly been caused by the action of the French Government. From this it necessarily follows that the French Government wishes that irritation to exist, but it does not necessarily follow that the French Government has resolved to go to war with this country. It may well be that a profound politician like the Emperor of the French is not unwilling to have it believed that his people are burning to avenge the misfortunes of the last war upon England, and that if peace be preserved it is entirely owing to his good sense and moderation. It may be that the Emperor Napoleon, while exciting the national spirit of

his subjects against us, and making such preparations as would be required if a war were really in contemplation, only means to place himself in so commanding a position that England, which desires peace above all things, may be intimidated into following whatever impulse he may please to give to the affairs of Europe ; or, lastly, it may be that these things really mean what those who are politically opposed to the Emperor declare they mean, and that we havo a danger to confront in the existence of which we cannot yet persuade ourselves to believe. Unhappily, we cannot afford to speculate on the alternative. The hatreds and passions of maukind are more easily stimulated than allayed, and it is not our fault if we are forced to act in a time of profound peace as if the camp of Boulogne was already formed again, and another flotilla awaited the orders of its Imperial master.

OltlTUAlCY It is with feelings of paiuful regret that we record the death of Kainmerraad Christian Frederik Bagger, Royal Bookkeeper, who departed this life this morning. Kammerraad Bagger arrived from Denmark, where ho was born on the 3rd Oct. 1807, in the year 1830, and from that year has been in Government's emplov, in which he rose step by step, and in 1857, was appointed Royal Bookkeeper. He also filled, diiriug his residence among us, many communal situations of trust and responsibility. By his kind and unassuming demeanour, he won the hearts and good wishes, not only of his own countrymen, but, we may freely say, of the entire native, and foreign population. We use not the language of the panegyrist, when we say, that his loss, to this community, is that of a truly good man. In regard to his official capacity, those only who have served under him can form a right opinion of his kindness and consideration for their welfare. Besides his bereaved widow, for whom he most tenderly cared, he has left a wide circle of friends whom he loved, and by whom bis memory will be cherished as one whom they trust to meet again in the realms of unfailing peace. His remains were interred this afternoon, followed by a large number of persons of all classes, thus testifying to the general esteem in which he wasjheld. Christiansted, Deo. 20, 1859.

From the Westminster Review WHAT KNOWLEDGE IS OF MOST WORTH. It has been truly remarked that, in order of time, decoration precedes diess. Before yet he thinks of protecting himself against the weather, the savage bestows much care on the painting of bisskiu." Among people who submit to great physical suffering that they may have themselves handsomely tattooed, extremes of temperature are borne with but little attempt at mitigation. Humboldt tells us that an Orinoco Indian, though quite regardless of bodily comfort, will yet labour for a lortnight purchase pigment to wherewith to make himself admired ; and that the same woman who would not hesitate to leave her hut without a fragment of clothing ou, would not dare to commit such a breach of decorum as to go out unpainted. Voyagers uniformly find that coloured beads and trinkets arc much more

prized by wild the cloths. And tribes than are calicoes or broad- auecdotes we have of the ways in which, when shirts and coats are given, they turn them to some ludicrous display, show how completely of the over that use. Indeed, the facts of aboriginal idea of ornament predominates life seem to indicate that drees is developed out of decorations. And when we remember that even among ourselves most think more about the fineness ot the fabric than its warmth, and more about the cut than the convenience þÿ when we see that the function is still in great measure subordinated to the appearance þÿ we have further reason for inferring such an origin. It is not a little remarkable that the like relations bold with the mind. Among meutal as among bodily acquisitions, the ornamental comes before the useful. Not only in times past, but almost as much in our own era, that kuowledge which conduces to personal well-being has been postponed to that which brings applause. In the Greek schools, music, poetry, rhetoric, and a philosophy, which, until Socrates taught, had but little bearing upon action, were the dominant subjects ; while knowledge aiding the arts j of life had a very subordinate place. And in our own universities and schools at the present moment the like antithesis holds. We arc guilty of something like a platitude whim we say that throughout bis after-career, a boy, iu nine cases out of ten, applies his Latin anil Greek to no practical purposes. The remark is tiite that

in his shop or his office, in managing his estate or his family, in playing his part as director of a bank or a railway, he is very little aided by this knowledge he took so many years to acquire ; þÿ so little, that generally the greater part of it drops out of his memery ; and if he occasionally vents a Latin quotation, or alludes the some Greek myth, it is less to throw light on to inquire what is the real motive topic in hand than for the sake of effect. If we a for giving boys classical education, we find it to be simply conformity to public opinion. Men dress their children's minds as they do their bodies, in the prevailing fashion. As the Oriuoco Indian puts on Iris paint before leaving his hut, not with a view to any direct benefit, but because he would be ash lined to be seen without it ; so, a boy's diiiling in Lnin and Greek is insisted on, not because of their intrinsic value, but that he may not be disgraced by being found ignorant of th na - that he may have "the education of a geuilcmian" þÿ the badge marking a certain social position, and bringing a consequent respect. in i his p arallel is still more clearly displayed the case of the other SaX. In the treatment of both an i lid rand body, the decorative element has continued to predominate in a greater degree among wutna u than among men. Originally, persouul adornment occupied the attention of both sexes equally. In these latter days of civilization, howeVvr, we see that iu the dress of men the regard for appearance has in a consider-

able decree Gelded to tire regard for comfort ' ; » while in their education the useful has of lato l beeu trenching on the ornamental. Iu neither direction lias this change gone so far with wouieu. The wearing of ear rings, finger-rings, bracelets; the elaborate dressings of the bair; the still occasional use of paint ; the immense labour bestowed in making habiliments suffi ciently attractive ; and the great discomfort that will be submitted to for the sake of conformity; show how greatly, in the attiring of women, the desire of approbation overrides the desire for warmth and convenience. And similarly in their education, the immense preponderance of " accomplishments" pioves how here, too, use is subordinated to display. Dancing deportment, the piano, singing, drawing þÿ what a large space do these occupy! It you ask why Italian and Gorman are learnt, you will find that, under all the sham reasons given, the real reason is, that at kuowledge of those tongues is thought ladylike. It is not that the books written in them may be utilized, which they scarcely ever are ; but that Italian and German songs may be sung, and that tire extent of attainment may bring whispered admiratioD. The births, deaths, and marriages of kings, and other like historic trivialities, are committed to memory, not beoause of any benefits that can possibly result from knowing them ; but because society considers them parts of a good education þÿ because the absence of such knowledge may bring the con-
tempt of others. When we have named reading, writing, spelling, grammar, arithmetic, and sewing, we have named about all the things a girl is taught with a positive view to their direct

Thoroughly to rea'iz the truth that with the mind as with (he body the or namental precedes the useful, it is needful to glance at its rationale. This lies in the facts that, f our tire far past down even to the present, social needs have sub- j ordioate individual i.e. is, and that tire chief social need has been the control of individuals. It is not, as we commonly suppose, that there are no governments but those ot inouaiclis, aud parliaments, and constituted authorities. These acknowledged governments are supplemented by other unacknowledged ones, that grow up in all circles, in which every man or woman strives to | ifolge Postanordningens IS Nr. 1 tilkorube king or queen or lesser dignitary. To get above some and be reverenced by them, and to propitiate those who are above us, is the universal struggle in which the chief energies of life are expended. 15y the accumulation of wealth, by style of living, by beauty of dress, by display of kuowledge or intellect, each tries to subjugate others ; and so aids in weaving that ramified network of restraints by which society is kept in j til alle Enkeltbreve, som ikke veie et fuldt order. It is not the savage chief only, who, iu formidable warpaint, with scalps at his belt, aims to strike awe into his inferiors ; it is not only t ie belle who, by elaborate toilet, polished j Breve, sotn veie over 1 Lod, eller som tor-

manners, and numerous accomplishments, strives to "make eouquests;'' but the scholar, the I historian, the philosopher, use their acquirements to the same end. We are none of us content with quietly unfolding our own individualities to the full iu all directions ; but have a restless craving to impress our individualities upon others, and in some way subordinate them. And this it is which determines the character of our education. Not what knowledge is of most real worth, is the consideration ; but what will bring most applause, honour, respect þÿ what will most conduce to social position and influence þÿ 11 is what will be most imposing. As, throughout j Forsendelseu, life, not what we are, but what we shall be thought, is the question ; so in education the question is, not the intrinsic value of knowledge, so much as its extrinsic effects on others. The Congress. þÿ The invitation is-ued by the Government of Fiance to attend a Congress of the European Powers has been received in London. The invitation from the Government of Austria has not yet arrived. The British Government will he represented iu the Congress. The appointed place of meeting is Paris. In many respects that selection is appropriate. If it is thought that the site may afford too great an advantage to the influence of one Power, it cannot he denied that the Emperor Napoleon has de facto taken the lead in the active prosecution of the Italian question. And the place of meeting is peculiarly convenient for the most direct, prompt, and constant communication beteen the British Government and its representative. The mere rumour of the Congress has occasioned a great and decided feeling of satisfaction. We are well aware that Sonic few in this country dislike to see England take any part in the Congress, and the motives for this feeling arc various. Certain members of a paity lately in power, which committed itself to the proposal of a Congress and then retracted, may not unnaturally regard with an invidious regret the opportunity uow afforded to a more consistent and generous statesmanship Some ultra-Conservatives are indiscriminately repugnant to anything which can prevent Austria from simply having her own way. A certain set object to everything ; and a lew honest " persons conscien- tiously fear that we may he drawn iu" to do loo much for the Italiaus. These arc not the

feelings of the great English community. The public can easily see that it would in no way promote the interests of this country to assume a position towards other Powers which would be tantamount to semi hostility. Such a position would particularly have that effect towards those States with whom we are on the most friendly relations. England would justly forfeit no small portion of her iuflueuce it she abstained from using it when she could employ it beneficially. For, perfectly disinterested, England can lend weight in sustaining such views as are ca ciliated to terminate unhappy and usless struggles, and to restore peace, on a basis consistent with events, with otir own piiuciples, and with the interests of all Europe. England will be the more able to perform this useful office since she enters the Congress unfettered by any rcst.aint whatsoever. We have already avowed our couviction that the Italians ought to he left to settle their own affairs in their own way, without external coercion ; and, in accepting a place at the proposed deliberative council of Europe, Euglana in no degree compromises the independence or freedom of her judgment þÿ Globe.

COMMUNICATION To the Editor of the St. Croix Ariis ! Sir ! Through tins medium I congratulate the catholic community of this I-land ou the auspicious event of receiving a long visit from such an illustrious personage, during this glorious season, as our pious and muck esteemed Bishop, Ilis Lordship the Right Reverend Doctor R jl. C PoiRiEK, who has been here since the 9th of this month. His Lordship administered the Sacrament of Confirmation in Chiistiansted on Sunday the lltlt to no postulants, and the following Sunday in Frederiksted to 94 His Lordship, otter administering Confirmation in this town, proceeded to Frederiksted and remained there until the 19th, where Mass was celebrated every morning and instructions and devotions held every evening, presided over by His Lordship. Mass and instructions in the evening were likewise given here in this parish, from the 20th to the morning of the 28th. Midnight mass was celebrated here Christmas Eve night at 12 o'clock by His Lordship, assisted by the Reverend Mr. Vabrkt, Chaplain, the Reverend Mr. ProST, Vicar General and Parish Priest, and the Reverend Mr. Krutill, Assistant Cure, at which 400 persons received the Holy Eucharist. A high pontifical Mass was tdso offered on Christmas Day at half past ten a. m. by His Lordship, which was attended by His Excellency Governor Schlegel and Lady and a very large congregation.

Having given a brief account, of these grand solemnities, which it has been the happiness of the parishioners both of Christiansted and Frederiksted to be present at, I will say a few words more as to the inttructions which were given in this Parish, and with regard to the proper and efficient manner in which everything was performed. Manv edifying, impressive and eloquent lectures were delivered by the parish priest and his assistant, to large congregations, who witli breathless attention listened to the good and pious .advices that w re ifered ; and on Christmas-day the Reverend Mr. Buggf.noms preached a very fine sermon. Too much praise cannot be bestowed on the Reverend Mr. Prost, the worthy and beloved rector of this parish, for the great care and pains evinced by him in imparting his duties to his flock, as a true disciple of Our Saviour, a'nd also to the Revd. Sir. Krutill, the assistant cure, during the short time he has been among us. The orderly manner in which everything was conducted, and t he nice music which was so well executed by the organist and choir, reflect great credit on these holy and eminent ministers. His Lordship took his departure from this Island this morning for St. Thomas, accompanied by the Reverend Mr. Vabret and the Reverend Mr. BugGE.N0.M8. Christiansted, 28th December 1859. T.

OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL. Fourth Session. THE 6th MEETING was held on Wednesday the 7th of December at 11 o'clock. The Chairman informed the Council, that he had received from the Governor the Landtreasury-accounts for St. Thomas and St. John's ) for 1855 to 1858. He presumed that the Assembly would proceed with respect to these accounts in the same manner as was done with those for St. Croix, and proposed the appointment of a committee of 2 members for that purpose. The Governor laid before the Council : 1. Draft of a Law relating to Navigation and j Trade in St. Thomas. This matter has already been discussed in a former session, but as circumstances have pre- I vented its being laid before the Diet, and possibly later experience may have suggested the expediency of proposing certain alterations in and additions to the dralt, it has be n deemed proper to bring the subject again before the Assembly. It will be seen from the explanatory rematks accompanying the draft, that a lew such additions are proposed, as for instance a reduction of the import duty on foreign colonial produce from 1£ per cent to a £ per tent. 2. Draft of an ordinance repealing 3 No. 10 of the ordinance of the 30th April 1824 concerning marriage s. The Council proceeded to the order of the day : 1. A petition front the Burgher Council of St. John's for the remission of the Landtreasury's debt to the Statetreasury &c. The 1st member for Christiansted's distiict þÿ Arnesen þÿ stated the circumstances which had given rise to the petition.

The amount on the books as due, amounts to about $12 or 13,000, of which a part, of pretty old stauding, <i< os not bear interest, and the remainder of more recent origin. The revenues of the island are small, owing to the great decrease of the cane cultivation since the emancipation. They amount altogether to about $450 or $500, and arc applied to schools, police, paupers See. There is not the most remote reasonable prospict of a total or even partial payment of the debt, and its continuance on the books has no other practical effect than to cause trouble and unnecessary correspondence, The petition furthermore states, the impossibility defraying of the expense of repairs of the Court-house, and refers to the necessity ap- of pointing ail lucassator and a Secretary for the business of the municipality. This office cannot be filled at a less remuneration than $150 p. a , which sum the Governor lias refused to sanction ; and as the members have not been willing to take this burden upon themselves personally without any remuneration, the Governor has withdrawn from them the management of the funds and caused the means in hand to be delivered over to the lloyul Treasurer in St. Thomas. Against these proceedings, which appear to bo somewhat harsh, the Burgher Council solicits the intervention of the Colonial Council. The Governor entered into a detailed .statement of the different items of which the debt in question consists, and stated as bis view of the case, that there arc parts of it which

ought and can be expected to be remitted, but he considers it quite certain, that, as to the remainder, the home-government will not acccdo cipally to the remission prayed for. The more recent part of the debt arises prin- from the establishment of the schools, _ and will in the beginning of next year amount to about $2,000. The amount which is not expected to be remitted is about $2500 to $3000. The Governor himself has laid the whole case and his views thereon before the Ministry, but has not yet received the answer. Regarding the salary for a Secretary and In cassator the Governor could not tbiuk it consistent with his duty to allow the sum of $150, or about 30 per cent of the whole revenue, to be applied for the collection of the same, and he had therefore proposed a percentage of 5 on

& T $ ® © I) X \ Hi h % % the amount collected as remuneration fur the office. lie acknowledged, that this would be but, a small payment, hut the amount from which it was to be drawn was proportionately small. It was only on the positive refusal of the Burgher Council to secure the performance of the duties in question, that lie f und himself under the necessity of providing for the performance of the business in another way. As for the repairs of the Courthouse, an arrangement had been made, by which the expenses were divided between the State Treasury, t he Countiy Treasury and the Judge of the island. The condition of the Country Treasury has improved in the last years, and is expected to improve still more, The 1st member for Christiansted's district þÿ Arnesen þÿ expressed his acknowledgment of the effoits of His Excellency to obtain a remission of the greater part of the debt, but could not admit the propriety retaining any part of of the debt as such against the island, after the cessation, without any hope of redemption, of the revenues, system a which may even deter any lish parties who might in future be willing to estab- in- themselves ill the. place and by their dustry contribute to the introduction of abetter state of things, from doing so. Neither could he feel himself satisfied with His Excellency's explanations of the. proceedings taken against the Burgher Council in the matter of the arrangement of the funds. He moved, that the Council would take the petition or such parts of it as its may appear wor- thy of their approval, under protection, and

proposed the appointment ot a committee of 3 members. The Governor pointed out, that he had not witlidrawu the management of the funds from the Burgher Council, but, that the latter had refused to continue the management unless on condition of the expense in question being sanctioned, and he is still willing to deliver it to them again, but not on the condition demanded. He has availed himself of the present vacancy of the office of the Judge to invest in the temporary occupier of the same the collection of the revenues f r a remuneration of 5 per cent, which measure having been brought to the notice of the Miuister, has obtained His Majesty's sanction by a r.>yal rescript of the 29th October last. This measure, it will be seen, Bad reference only to the collection of the revenues, but in no manner interferes with the right < f t lie Burgher Council to regulate the affairs of the municipality. The 2nd member for St. John's þÿ Hill þÿ considered the collection of revenues by t he Judge as not quite consistent with the position of a Judge, and observed, that the charge of 5 per cent had only reference to t lie duties of the Iucassator, but not to those of the Secretary ; and even in respect to the collection alone, he tain thought that the arrangement would a to a cer- measure be accompanied with pressure on some of the poorer tax-payets. The 1st member for Christiansted's district þÿ þÿAinesen was of the opinion, that, according to the Law concerning the Burgher Councils,

the matter ought to have been laid before the home-government before being cariied into execution, as it did not imply any new expense. i Burgher Council of St John's. The Governor replied, that it was a new it from the beginning. He had change made in 1856, and that ho not had left opposed out of view the other duties in question besides those of the Incassitor, and the payment undoubt- is edly a mere trifle in comparison with the labor to "be performed ; hut if the remuneration was to be rated on the principle of that comparison, it would not be exorbitant to fix it at the total amount of tho revenues. The motion for a Committee was adopted with 8 votes against 5. 2. The draft of tho Budget. The 1st member for Frederiksted's district þÿ Castonier moved, þÿ that a Committee of 5 be elected to examine and report on the draft. The 1st member for Christiansted's district þÿ ArneseD þÿ observed, that it had been the custom on former occasions to subject tho draft to a general discussion of the Assembly before the appointment of a Committee. 12 The motion was rejected by votesagainst 1.

The 1st member for Ghristiansted's district þÿ Arueseu þÿ remarked that the natural difficulties atlendiug the discussion of the Budget bad been iucr ased by the delay, contrary to the Colonial Law, for 3 years in the convocation of the Council. The general contents of the Budget are pretty much the same as the former ones, which is the more to be deplored, as the state of things in this island as well as in St. John's, and perhaps even in St. Thomas, has retrogaded, and as it is consequently necessary to examine closely whether there are not, among t he expenditure, items whioh might be reduced. In the revenue for St. Croix in particular there is oqe .item which cannot lie passed over, viz : the Customs- dues, where the import-duty shows a revenue of upwards of $40,000, and the export duty of upwards of $50,000. The first of these sums cannot bo Said to be high, considering the number ot inhabitants upon whom it falls; the export-duty on the other hand becomes a heavy burthen upon the produce as soon as the properties, f.om which it is drawn, do not yield a sufficient revenue to cover their expenses, as has been the case the last 2 or 3 years with a number of them. The evil effects of the export-duty in general are still more injurious, if we look to tho export-duty to foreign countries ; for in addition to the immediate loss thrown on ti e produce, it acts as an impediment to the natural trade of the island, and thereby raises the prices on the necessary articles of

consumption. The loss in the revenue that might be apprehended from a tepeal of this part of the duty may he expected to be covered by retrenchments in the expenditute. Another ol jrctionable source of revenue is the Auction-fees. The 1st mernbi r fur Fredeiik-ti d's district þÿ Sarauw þÿ sided on the whole with the lemarks made by the preceding speaker, but must differ with regard to some expressions made by him on the feasibility of raising the import-duty on certain articles. The honorable member spoke disapprovingly of several items of expenditure. - Particularly concerning the court-fi. es hi; r< marked, that a Commission appointed for the purpose has already several years ago drawn up a detailed plan of their adjustment ; furthermore the fees for pass ports to fort ign countries, the exorbitance of which had caused a diminution in the revenue, by leading people to take out pass-ports to St Thomas only, where the charge is less, and there take a new pass-port to the place of their destination. The 5th member for Christianstcd's district þÿ Rothe þÿ spoke against the double export-duty on produce shipped to foreign countries. The 2d member for St. John's þÿ Hill þÿ stated his intention of moving an amendment concerning the export-duties ft out that island, arid a re-establishment of the mail-boat form rly em ployed between St. John's and St. Thomas. The discussion of the Bndget was adjourned, after which the Council appointed a Committee to examine and r port on the Country Treasury-

Beatty , saddler in this town.

The Liverpool correspondent of the Manchester Guardian writes Nothing definite transpired on Saturday relating to the correspondence between four gentlemen in Liverpool and the Emperor of the French. It is stated, however, that the letter in question was written by the four gentlemen while enjoying the pleasures of a þÿ full þÿboard one evening, about a fortnight since. Nothing serious was dreamt of ; the letter was posted, but a reply was never anticipated. So little was the affair thought of that a copy of the letter to the Emperor was not even kept, and the whole matter was looked upon as a good joke. Judge of the consternation of these four gentlemen when, on Friday, they received a letter in reply to theirs, written by an official four could read, as it was written in the French language. I am not aware that any suggestion has been held out to the diplomatists about to meet in Congress at Paris that they should begiu operations upon the destinies of Italy by a prolonged tour throughout the Peninsula. This couutry has been a riddle to negotiators ever since the time that its people laid the first rudiments of the art of diplomacy, and when no less than 16 Florentines sat at the same council-board as legates or ambassadors of as many European potentates. Ono of the most scheming minds of the present day, the Emperor Napoleon, and his advisers, have been for the last 10 or 11 months working in the daik, and acting upon an estimate of the Italiau character which has proved to be signally erroneous by events. Indeed, in his efforts to settle Italy by war or peace, Napoleon 111 must avow he has gone through a series of grievous disappointments. He expected, it seems, that every Italiau, like every Frenchman, would muster as a soldier at his beck, aud when he found the people, as he thought or said, slack in the war, he relii d at least on their full acquiescence in the peace. He settled and sold them at Villalranca and Zurich as it best suited him, and held them as amenable to his pleasure as the 8,000,000 of Frenchmen who elected him to the Empire. Napoleon III. has misconceivi d the Italians, as he must avow, and it were well if the statesmen who are soon to assemble under his presidency oould be put on their guard against the same, or

even worse, mistakes. Were the Italians to have a voice in the Congress, undoubtedly their plan for a settlement of all their difficulties would poiut to the utter exclusion of Austria from her last stionghold of Venetia and the Southern Tyrol; to the union of at least the whole valley of the Po, from the Alps to the Tagliatnento and the Tavollo, into a northern kingdom under King Victor Emmanuel II. ; to the utter abolition of the temporal power of the Pope, to whom not an inch of ground would be left beyond the precincts of the Vatican and St. þÿPeter s; aud to the organization of Central Italy south of the Apennines, Naples and Sicily, into two States, leagued with, or dependent on, the great northern kingdom. There is no doubt in my mind but that such an arrangement would best meet the strong tendencies of the Venetians, Parmesans, Modenese, and Romagnese for union. It would best gratify the somewhat municipal instincts of the Tuscans,

(L l! H Hj ll $5 «! and would satisfy the universal craving of the whole nation for independence, for the best possible fusion, and for thorough emancipation from priestly thraldom From some talk I have heard, which I consider sufficiently important to deserve attention, 1 should judge that the scheme with which Austria and France intend to appear before Congress is somewhat as follows : þÿ Austria to give up Venetia, to he governed as an þÿ independent State by the Archduke Ferdinand of þÿTuscauy, an þÿ independence which should not, however, of course, withdraw the State from Imperial Austrian protection; Parma, Modena, and Tuscany to he united iu one State under the sceptre of a Prince (French or Ru.-bian ), to be appointed by Congress ; the Legations to return to the allegiance of the Pontiff; this latter, it is well understood, to adopt such reforms as would reconcile his subjects to his rule, and render a foreign occupation unnecessary. It would he well, I repeat, if, before they come to their deliberations on some motion of this nature, the Paris negotiators would take the Corbie to study the Italian question by personal observation. It would be well if they tefi c ed what the resolutions of previous congresses, at Vienna, Verona, and Laybach, have led the world to. Austria had at those meetings the mission to crush Italy intrusted to her, and the result has been to drive her to the very last corner of the Peninsula. By the co operation of France the crushing work may, no d >ubt, be earned oil for

a lew more years; but, admitting even the possibility of a really good understanding and combined action between two such rival Powers, there is little doubt but the Italy of 1868 would become as unmanageable to the two empires as the Italy of 1S48 or 1859 had proved to one of them. To beat the Italians in the field is, iudeed, too easy a work. Notwithstanding the steady gallantly of the Piedmontese, aud the dashing impetuosity of þÿGaribaldi s bauds, the Italians are as yet an unwarlike race, though those successive revolutions have been rapidiy hardening them as if by fire. 8o long as they are enslaved and divided they will certainly never improvise armies fit to cope with either French ardour or German steadfastness. Ev.u militarily, however, Italy has made great pioþÿgress, the valour of the Savoyard has becorno the common heritage of the Piedmontese; Piedmontese drill will now bring the Milanese into the held. Still, it is not iu horses or iu chariot that Italian nationality is uow, or will for some time he, able to put its trust. Ita y it never less beaten than when she is beaten in the field; aud I do not hesitate to assert that Veiled i is at the present moment less under the moral control of Austria than Lombardy is. It is necessary to travel through that province, or, even bettor, to visit the cities ol Central Italy, to see where lies the real strength of the country. It is necessity to count the multitudes, of both sexes, of all ages and conditions running away

from Austrian þÿ clemency, protesting agaiu-t Imperial amnesties, bearing witness before Europe that Austria may have the couutry, but cuiiuot have the people The emigration fever which has seized on the whole Venetian population lias now spread to the Tiontine or South Tyrolean territory. Those Italiau Tyrolese were proverbially loyal and subservient t > Austrian interests. Among them the Imp rial Government tumid s tine of her bravest light troops, the magistrates, police officers, sbirri, and gaolers, all willing instruments to subdue tliei. Loin birdo-Veuetiau fellow -subjects. Now, lo ! I South Tyrol refuses point-black to send her men of trust to the Innsbruck Congregation ; the Trentines loudly protest they are Italians, and if they cannot he allowed lo join their happy country-men in emancipated Lombardy, tney will at least share the hard fate of their countrymen iu enslaved Venice. Like their Venetian lellow-sufferers they migrate en masse ; they exchange the free air of their beloved mountains lor the noisome confinement of the cities of tlio þÿplain- their unfettered pursuits as hunters or shepherds for the irksome duties of a þÿsoldier s life. All this is a new and important phase iu the annals of Italian revolution. Compelled to look for reluge abroad up to 1848, no Italian left home, except under the pressure of imminent personal danger. Exile was to their than views au evil hardly less to bo dreaded narrow imprisonment; but now expatriation has lost its
worst terror. South of the Po or west of the Minoio there is still a country, a home for the Venetian or the Treuline. Lands may be sold,

money may be carried about or remitted ; every man whose legs can hear him, every family whose means can support them ; will quit Venice, and even to the poor and needy the help of their brethren of Milan or Turin will not fall short. What will amnesties or mild and conciliatory measures avail Austria? What good can Congress achieve by awarding ail Italian province to an Austrian Archduke, under tho specious form of a nominal independence ? Austiia must either go, or the Venetians and Trentines will. Congress may set a price upon those provinces; it may decide to what extent ail the freed provinces ofltaly may, for the sake of peace, he drained to their last penny, to the value of their last picture, of their last artistic woik or antiquarian relic ; but it cannot contrive a scheme which will enable Austria to do more than loid it over a desert. The exodus is in full tide; it lias broken forth before the doom of tho country is clearly resolved upon ; it will acquire fresh speed and intensity at every effort that may be made to render that doom irrevocable. If the sale of Venice and Trent is the best project with which Austria may appear before the Congress at Pari-, there is no doubt hut the best proposal with which France may open proceedings will be her renunciation of the patronage she now exercises over Rome, and evidently hopes to extend to all the Roman provinces. The Romagnese will not, perhaps, upon a te-toratiou of the Papal authorities, all migrate en masse, like t ie Venetians ; hut they will certainly

prove even le-.s pliable than these latter. The self-victory that these people have for the last ten mouths obtained over themselves will, no doubt, enable them in the end to overcome any adversary. They have upon calculation made their country as still as a convent of monks ; they will have it in their power upon provocation to turn it into a den of wild beasts It is necessary to travel through the laud, to mingle with the people of all classes, in older to become aware of the deep roots that hatred of priestly rule has struck throughout the Legations. It is necessary to see the daily food that the press of these countries supplies to popular animosity to imagine the outbreak that will inevitably foiiow any removal ol the chock that hope ol uetti r destinies still puts upon the pa siuns of the multitude. Even in this milder and less ill used Tuscany, politic- h.ve b come mi all-engio-sing þÿtopic- a fever, a mania, and every man hangs on the slightest breath of news with uu earnestness which is no less painlul than inatvellous to behold. But in the Romagna expectation has something more dogged and sullen, something more reckless aud desperate. There is in these people a determination to leave nothing unattempted to win the goodwill of Europe. ol They thiuk they ought to do all for the pi nee Europ , so long as Europe may be induced to do anything iu justice to them ; hut the mono lit a a European Congress pronounces in favour u! Papal restoration, no matter upon what terms of

reform or secularization, they will he quit of all duty; they will deem themselves entitled to do their worst; they will deal by Europe as they have been dealt with. They may not be strong enough to resist Austria, France, or tin 200,000- 00.) of Oati.olies the Pope fancies lie has in his p iy ; but the Pope, and all the þÿPope a s llies, wid Dot he able so to keep them undo restraint as to afford t lie world that peace which Congress I meets to establish on broad and safe bases. The policy of that þÿPow er agaiust þÿAustria at Klattseuburg, has in Transylva- always been to weaken Hungary by stirring up strife between the different nationalities established in her territory ; aud in 1848-9 she succeeded but too well in exciting the Saxons of Transylvania to hostility against their parent State. But these people have long since seen the error of their ways, and have become heartily reconciled to the rist of Hungary. Well, they had, on some local occasion, a grand banquet at Ivlausenburg the other day, and their foremost men delivered speeches, the burden of which was eulogism of

the Hungarian nation, regret that the Saxons had ever allowed themselves to be led into hostility to it, and the promise that henceforth they will act in all things as members of the great Hungarian people. Toasts in accordance with the speeches were dtunk with enthusiasm. þÿ December 8. þÿ I am able to inform you that the Viennese Cabinet is so seriously alarmed at what The Times and other English journals have said respecting the oppression of the Protestants in Hungary, that Count de Reehberg, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, has deemed it necessary to address a circular to the Austrian diplomatic agents at foreign Courts directing them to give explanations on the subject to the different Governments. 1 have not yet obtained a copy of this circular, but I am told tl at its contents aie to this effect: þÿ The Austrian Government thinks that the Hungarian Protestants have no just reason to complain of oppression, inasmuch as the Imperial patent regulating their worship, which it issued some months ago, is, in its eyes, of a reasonably liberal character. Nevertheless, as that patent is decidedly unpalatable to the Protestauts, the Government might, perhaps, have consented to modify it or even replace it altogether, if that the but they insist ou would have satisfied them ; pure and simple re-establishment of their soil-government and independence as they existed pieviously to 1848. Now, to grant anything of this kind would be an abandonment of the Bacb-Schwnrzenbeig policy

of investin'1 in the, hands of the central Government the sole and uncontrolled regulation of all public þÿmatters a policy which has been practised for years, and which the Government cannot and will not abandon or modify. Count de Ilechberg therefore hopes that foreign Governments will see that the Hungarian Protestants are putting forth utterly unreasonable pretensions, and that consequently no attention will be paid to what newspapers may say about their grie vanet s þÿ will I only sav one word in answer to this Austrian circular, and that is, that the Austrian Government bad neither a moral nor legal light to deprive the Hungarian Protestant Church ol liberties aud immunities which it had enjoytd for centuries, and which are ab-olutely necessary for the defence tf the faith in >i» it purity', and for the maintenance of discipline. This being so, it follows that if the Hungaiiun Piotestants were to submit without a inuunur to the tyranny to which men ol the Bach and fclehwaizenbeig ntiil Reehberg class think they ought to be subjected, they would be veritable þÿcravens a disgrace to thi ir teligion aud their race. < While the Viennese Cabinet is thus trying to prejudice European Governments against the Protestants of this country, it has begun persecuting the Protestants with a high hand. At Pesth, Presburg, Miskolez, Ksesmaik, and several other places, the police have made visits to the houses of leading Protestants, and have seized all their piiyate pip rs; they have also

commenced a prosecution of seveial iiiflu ntial gentlemen and charge of þÿ exciting to discontent against the s me reverend ministeis, on the þÿGovernment. The ground on which the charge is based is, that the gentlemen and clergymen have taken a leading part in the opposition which has been manifested to the Imperial patent. But, without stopping to remark that it was a sacred duly for them to oppose a measure which they tnought injurious to their leligion, it must he noted that the Austrian Government it elf, in issuing the patent, actually requested the Protestants to communicate tin ir observations upon it ! It is only in a country under Austrian d ruination that an act soabsuid and yet so odious as the prosecution ot men tor doing the very' thing the Government þÿitself requested them to do could be perpetrated. « Another not less striking example of the scandalous tyranny ct the Viennese Cabiuet can be recorded. You are, perhaps, aware that though the cultivation of tobacco is one of the most profitable things farmers in this country can engage in, the Austrian Government arrogates to itself the power of saying annually that so many acres, and no more, shall be planted with tobacco. These three things will appear passably exorbitant in English eyes, but

CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, J7th JANUARY, 1S60. þÿ þÿ THE proceedings of the Coloni I Council, in its present Session, are certainly more interesting than we remember to have remarked before. More sober truths, in favor of Colonial Rights, against the selfish policy of the Home- Government, have been uttered, in this Session, than have ever resounded through the Council-Hall. The Government, it is generally said, has met with more opposition than it expected. The po I icy of the mother-country, to grant only those wishes of the colonies which accorded with its own previously-formed intentions, has, no doubt, awakened a desire to test the value and power of the Colonial Council. If the Council were merely intended to echo the wishes of the Government, then, we should say, the manner in which the representations of the Council, on manv subjects of interest and benefit to the Colonies, have been passed over in silence, would warrant that course of proceediug on the part of the Government; but the institution was never viewed in that light by the majority of the Colonists, and we therefore rejoice to see that an opportunity now presents itself to judge of the real value of the institution, by the manner in which the representations that have, and will be, made in this Session, will be received by the Home- Government.

The Postal-Law has received such treatment, in this Session, as would, in a free-country, unquestionably settle its fate. The Committee-Report partakes more of the nature of a censure than an advice. Speaking of the 20 per cent, postage on newspapers, to vernment now proposes which the Go- reduce to 10 per cent., tlu Committee remarks : þÿ We are sorry to find that the Government has taken so little notice of the advice of the Colonial Council in its last Session, viz.: to allow Newspapers and Periodicals to he forwarded tree of postage between the Danish Islands and the towns of St. Croix, that this has not even been granted to the two papers that, twice a week, are issued in these Islands, a boon that would have been of great importance to the editors of these Papers, and ot very little consequence to the þÿPost-chest. It may, perhaps, create a smile, when we inform our readers, that the whole amount of revenue derived through the postage on this paper, and which the Government is so unwilling to relinquish, does not amount to twenty dollars pr. annum. The reduction proposed by the Government, being a percentage on the yearly amount of the subscription, not affect us for better; since, we would forward our papers, in a closed package to West-End to be there distributed, and thus have to pay according to weight ; and by which course we effect a saving ot sixty cents yearly to each subscriber. Only on three papers, forwarded to St. Thomas, would the proposed reduction have an apparent, yet not real, effect ;

for, the postage, being now two cents on each paper, is paid, in our present currency, by one stiver; while, should the postage be reduced to one cent, we should still have to pay that cent by a stiver. On the whole, we cannot but consider the Postal Law as too grand concep- a tion for us, poor West Indians ; especially when we consider, that all its advantages are on one side ; and that, instead of the Post Office being a convenience, it is, in many respects, complained of as a public grievance.

Many of the names they contain are household words. Some are the names of Europeans, others of West Indians, and even Asiatics. Barely a third of the public debt is held in this country. The bulk of it, we imagine, is held in Continental Europe One is not surprised to find the name ot John J. Astor, W. B. Astor, Jacob Little, G. Peabody, and such men in the list ot the creditors of the United States, but they and their countrymen are creditor nority. The heaviest foreign in a miwe noticed is Lord Overstone (the famous J ties Loyd), who has lent this country no less than $250,000. A Spanish lady, Merced de Laseea, is our creditor to the tune ot 200,000, and a noble friend of hers, the Count Casa Montlovoy Castillo, draws (5 per cent, on $100,000. Several persons connected with the Royal families of Europe are creditors of ours. The brother ot the King ot Naples took $50,000 some years ago, and instructed his agent to invest the dividends as they accrued in the same security. He now owns over $75,000. Ilis niece, the daughter of Bomba, is registered as a creditor for over 50,000. These wise people have been looking out tor a rainy day. Another noble personage, the late Duchess of Orleans, has enough in the United States to save the Count of Paris from

being compelled to follow his grandþÿfather example s and keep school. Several of the Saxe-Coburg Gothas have also invested in the same country. The Count Rossi saw enough of this country while he was here to invest a few thousands in the famous name of Sontag, and little Paul Julien has a tr, lie-enough to keep him when his violin fails. One can readily account for the appearance of the name of the Rothschilds, both ot London and Paris; but it is curious that the famous publisher, Panchonke, ot Paris, is a creditor of the United States; and that the dramatic author, Scribe, has also invested enough to give him nearly 10, OOOf. in a America of democracy year. A careful study appears to have persuaded Tocqueville to lodge some M. of his savings in the hands ot our Government ; Lord Macaulay, who began with a bagatelle of some 5,000 has since increased his venture to nearly $30,000. But we shall never end if we attempt to enumerate all the people who have their money placed in the United þÿStates securities. Here are Lord Dundonald, the great sailor, who has a large sum for a son of Neptune; the Prince de Beauven, the Count de Narbonne, Sir John Baylcy, the Marquis of Champagne, Baring Brothers, Count de Beaumont, General Bermelotl, and a host ot titled people, who, perhaps, depend upon the honesty and solvency of the United Stales Government lor a living. Lord Elgin saw enough of us to leave 17,000 of his savings in our Six per Cents., and the famous Russian, Alex-

andre Herzen, has a bagatelle of 80,000 in the same security. There is another creditor, whose name is a curiosity. It runs thus þÿ Baron Louis Numa Epaminondas Justinian Aristides Decius Satis Haldenstein Leichenstein Gortenstein. Fancy a man with such a name drawing twenty-six dollars and fitly cents from the United þÿStates. Philadelphia Ledger, Nov. 18.

The Council proceded to : 1st discussion of the draft of an ordinance extending to the Danish Westindia Possessions the ordinance of the 7th March 1827 and the placard of the 3rd March 1841, concerning þÿlawyers -fees in the Upper Court in Copenhagen &c , in criminal suits. The 3id crown-member þÿ Stakemann recommended the draft as simply carrying into effect a clear principle of justice, explaining at the same time, the unfavorable positiou generally in which the legal profession are placed at present in these colonics, judges as well as lawyers, which has already shown its effects iu the disinclination of competent persons to ap-

ply for the situations becoming vacant, and which threatens to load to a want of practising lawyers. With regard to the details of the draft, he had only one objection to make, viz : against 4, as containing a new sanction of the rule in 42 of the ordinance of the 3rd June 1796, a rule most unjust iu principle, as it threw oyer a burden, which properly lies on the public, on a third party, namely : the opponent of the party in the suit who has obtained the benefit of gratuitous pleadings, merely on account of the benefit thus grained, and in cases where the opponent, although losing the case, could not on general principles have been coudemm d to pay the costs. The 1st member for þÿFrederiksted district s Sarauw þÿ supported the views and statements of tho pieceding speaker. The 1st no mber for þÿChristiansted district s Arnesen þÿ opposed the measure, both on ac count of the expense it will cause to the Country Treasury, and on the grounds of the small labor which the conduct of most of the public suits require. With regard to the justice of the measure he observed, that the lawyers had received their licenses to practice subject to the condition of carrying on the public suits without pay, and they have therefore no right to complain. The 5th member for þÿChristiansted sdistrict --Rothe þÿ strongly recommended the measure, insisting upon the great public advantages, which these colonies owed to the exertions of practising lawyers, and deploring the scarcity of lawyers at the present time. As regards di-

vers observations of the preceding speaker he warned the Assembly against attaching too much weight to tho deprecatory remarks brought and tho working of the Danish laws and spirit forward on several occasions against the institutions. He also had bestowed care and attention on the nature of the laws and legal in-

stitutions of other countries, and although well aware of the deficiencies of those of Denmark, he expressed it as his full conviction, that they were, to say the least of it, by no means greater than those of other countries The 2d member for þÿChristiansted district s þÿ Heyliger þÿ wished to know the probable amount of the expenses to he incurred by the change, and expressed his sense of the injustice of the present system. The Governor referred for the information desired to the motives accompanying the draft. The 3d þÿcrown-member Stnki þÿmanu in reply to the remarks made by the 1st member for Christiansted þÿ Arn< sen þÿ stated, that every one of those objections had been equally valid in Denmark 30 years ago, when the existing regulations wore made, and that the want of funds could not be opposed with propriety, when it was notorious, that there exists a considerable surplus in the Oountry-Tieasury, and that it is in consequence under discusssion to reduce certain taxes to the same. þÿ If it is true, tnat in many cases the labor is small, it will also be found that the amount of the pay, as fixed in the draft, is small. With regard to the objection, that the lawyers had taken their commission under the condition ol bestowing their labor for the public without remuneration ; the same < bj etion will hold good against the reduction or abolition of taxes on propeities acquired, subj ct to iho.-e taxes. The 5th member for Christiansted þÿsdistiict þÿRothe -stated, that he would move an amend-

ment in the form of tho draft, which he proposed to be worded as follow s, viz : þÿ The ordinance of tin 7th March 1827 þÿ þÿ and the placard of the 3rd Maich 1841 concorning salaries to lawyers in public suits are extendi d to the Danish W. stindia Posþÿ þÿ sessions for the lawyers practising at the Upper-and Lower-Court.-, in such a man- "ner, that the fees are limited to five Westþÿ india dollars in small and simp'e cases, hut þÿ in more extensive cases are raised till fifþÿ teen þÿdollars. He observed, that this appears to be the most natural and appropiiate form, and is the one which has been universally employed since 1821, and is most in accordance with the 21 in the Colonial-law. He considered, that even in the case of smaller laws, the form of embodying the whole con-' tents of the law in the draft, instead of merely referring to the existing law, which it is proposed extend to the colonies, can h ad to a to deviation from the latter, which had not been intended, but the consequences may be much worse, when the question is applied to laws of considerable magnitude. The only instance in which the present form was adopted, was, to the best of the memory of the speaker, the ordinance for extending to the colonies the ordinance of the 21st May 1845, and the consequence was, that it became necessary to rectity, by a special Reset ipt, the errors and omissions committed. motive for proposing the amendment to principal The honorable member stated his be, tho

regret he felt in seeing so much ability and learning spent on these small drafts, which would have been employed with infinite advantage on the many urgent subjects of necessary reform in our own internal affairs. The Governor expressed his opinion, that tho matter moved by the honorable member had already been decided on a former occasion iu this session, and explained that the instance derived from the publication of the ordinam c of the 21st May 1845 wa» not applicable ; but that the form now complained of had been foil wed by the authorities in Denmark, as a proof of which he referred to the law lately passed for an alteration of the coinage.
