S'-. þÿ An agitation, which is on the tapis, having for its object the removal and depot from St. Thomas to s some ot the Royal Mail þÿCompany s teamships contiguous and more healthy port, leads one to consider the cause þÿ which makes the present station unhealthy. I am not about to enter into a scientific elucidation of the mystery, hut to take a common sense view of the subject. considered a land-locked harbour, fairly The port of St. Thomas may lie surrounded by high hills, enclosing an area of something less than a square mile of water, entirely pent in, and rendered semi stagnant from the want of that circulation essential to the purity of sea water. 1 lie prevailing winds are from northeast to east and south-east lo sou h the ; latter wind blows directly into the harbour, and the easterly wind across its base. The current from the oiling passes the þÿharbour mouth, s and is diverted into the Last Gregorie channel, because Sprat Point, on Water simpiv Isl nil, extends more to the southward than þÿDowell Point, s intercepting the stream which nearly always runs lo the westward. I his will account for the waters ia tile harbour being seldom changed. As the north-east wind is most prevalent, it has the effect of forcing down of surface water, loaded with portion to the lee side ol the harbour a debris, garbage, and other impurities, to undergo decomposition al the coal wharves, ca-

reening hole, and the swampy land adjoining and under Careen-hill ; lint the most important fact is the daily addition to thc sheet of water from the surface and open drainage of the town occupied by 15,000 inhabitants, vegetable and other matters washed down from the hills by every shower of rain ; in fact, the harbour is the grand receptacle of every impurity, both from the shipping ajid from the shore, and the town of Charlotte Amalie may well he thankful for the frequency of its rains ns the sole cause of its healthiness as with the shipping in its ports. compared 1 he fact of the harbour being impure cannot for a moment he doubted. Contrast the colour of the two waters (divided as they are by a narrow ledge of locks), those of the Gregorie being limpid and of ocean colour, while those ol the harbour are of n poor sickly green tinged with yellow. Is not this ample testimony ? 1 lie evaporation of this sheet of impure water is, in my humble opinion, t he cause of the prevalence of yellow (ever. Willi a southerly or hot wind it. is increased; with the more refreshing north-east winds it is retard. !. Were it possible to drain the liarbo .1 expose its putrid bed to the sun . iv >. the destruction to life from mi sn. ,\. ild be more terrible than that told of the fable of the upas-tree valley. The moving of any or flie numerous vessels and steamers from one bour to another, has the part effect of dis- of the harturbing the under-stratum of water, and bringing it under the immediate action

of the sun, to evaporate in baneful exare more halations. Uhe proofs nf its convincing when the ropes impurity nnd hawsers are hauled in loaded with a slimy matter, offensive and nauseous in the highest degree. Can the superincumbent matter lie pure over such a bed i

There can be no doubt as to the fact of the southern winds increasing the evaporation, but it has also a most enervating effect upon the human frame, predisposing it to the attack of that dreadful scourge, yellow fever, generated and strengthened by the oppressive heat of the wind. It is, indeed, no misnomer to call it the fever wind. To render my hypothesis stronger, I venture to assert that the shipping suffer in a much greater ratio than the town by the visitation of the rows the subject to fever ; this fact nar- shipping, and it is obvious that both cause and effect lie there. Can any one say the Transatlantic steamers bring fever into the port ? Yet, albeit, the majority of the crews are acclimatised, and few, if any, have communication with the shore; the fever, latent for awhile, breaks out and deals around to its victims sickness and death. The cause of all this, I assert, is the inhalation of the vapours arising from the impure waters of the harbour. The remedy to purify this sheet of water is hv creating a current in the harbour by artificial means. This result, I am of small channel across the þÿ opinion, can lie effected by cutting þÿ þÿHaulover a the ledge of rocks before spoken of, which lie even with the þÿwater edge s at high water. It should be deep enough to receive the lower stratum of water, at least twenty feet wide, tapering on the Grcgorie side to ten feet, so that the greater resistance should be on the harbour sitle, in order that its waters may

be attracted by the slight current of the Grcgorie and carried away to seaward through the West Grcgorie channel. The prevailing winds setting in this direction would have a very beneficial effect in forcing the water down to this part of the harbour, and through the outlet-. This portion of the harbour being, as it were, a sink to the port, should undergo a complete dredging, the necessity for which will sooner or later be imperative. Thus a few thousand dollars judiciously expended in cutting the canal, the accomplishment of which presents no engineering difficulties whatever, would at once create a current, and by cleansing the harbour would, to say the least, be a movement in the right direction, checking the existence of fever by imparting a purer tone to its waters. The Island of St. Thomas, abutting on the Atlantic, and washed by the Carribean Sea, enjoys an ocean breeze, and cannot of itself be unhealthy. Yellow fever is rarely found in any other part of the island than its harbour. There alone lies the seat of the disease, and it is but natural to conclude that the town ! attending on Stock kept at cannot alwav s escipe the dire effects of the impure vapours of the harbour I have learnt with much satisfaction that the subject of the canal has already been mooted by one of the commanders of the Royal Mail þÿCompany ships, s and that it has reached official quarters, and I trust no time will be lost ere the experiment is tried. I cannot, however, forego the hope that by keeping up the

attention to this subject it may, if necessary, be more fully discussed or my suggestion at once acted upon, so that having removed, or even mitigated the cause of yellow fever in the port of St. Thomas, it may be boldly and safely asked, where is there a better harbour for the Royal Mail Steamers to rendezvous? INTER-COLONIAL NEWS. At Grenada there had been an inspection of the Forts and Fortifications by Major General Cloete and his Staff, accompanied by the Governor, Mr. Kortright, on the 20th December, and afterwards a review of the Volunteer Artillery and Rifle Corps ; on which occasion the Major-General is said to have observed, þÿ that of all the Militia Bodies he had seen in these Islands, the St. þÿKitt s Cavalry and the Grenada Artillery Corps ranked foremost for discipline and effectiveness ; and that should Government come to the decision of sending out any portion of the þÿQueen Troops s to this Island, there would be no necessity for Artillerymen in addition to the Volunteers now doing duty þÿhere. His Excellency and Staff left on the following day to proceed to Trinidad on his tour of inspection. The past fortnight had been taken up with the usual Examinations of the Public and Private Schools, viz , the Lamolie House Academy, þÿ private a establishment of great þÿmerit, conducted by Mr. Comissiong; the Wesleyan Schools of St. George and Constantine, on the 20th ; the Roman Catholic School, St. þÿGeorge s on the 21st ; and the Normal and Grammar School on the 22ud. þÿ The þÿresult, says the Chronicle, þÿ has been generally highly gratifying, and the Colony may be congratulated upon the possession of as good and successful Schools, as any part of II. M. Colonial þÿPossessions. What with these Juvenile Exhibitions, gratifying as they always are to those who witness them, and especially to the relatives of the Pupils,

and the visit of General Cloete and his Staff, the review of the Volunteer Corps, festivities, the firing of salutes, and the Christinas we can well believe that þÿ the fortnight has resembled one continued Christmas þÿEve. At Demerara, the proposal of the Governor in the Court of Policy, that the whole cost of Immigration (75 head) should be defrayed by the i whom the Immigrant is assigna portion of it (50 dollars) by him, and the remainder out of the Public Treasury, as heretofore, had given rise to much excitement in that body against the scheme. The object of the Governor is to remove the objection to the Immigration System entertained by the Anti-Slavery Party and other persons of influence in England ; and he proposes to compensate the Planters by abolishing the duties paid by them on coals, lumber, &c The question has not yet been decided by the Court. The Action for Libel brought by the Inspector of Police against the Creole Newspaper, for charging him with having used the Police for his own private benefit, in various Police Stations in the Rural Districts, and with using the provender furnished for the use of the Police Horses to feed his Stock, had, after a trial of six days, terminated in a verdict for the Plaintiff, damages one dollar, (they were laid at 5000 dols.,) each party to pay his own costs ; which we should consider here a very damaging verdict for the Plaintiff, as much as to say that he had better not have brought his action. Ten convicts escaped from Cayenne a i few days ago, in an open boat, and among the number was Carlo de Rudio who was sentenced to hard labour for life for his share in the Orsini plot to assasinate the Emperor Louis Napoleon in Feb. 1858. They were confined on the Cayenne. Having made a small preliminary island near arrangemenfs for their escape, they seized

a favourable opportunity, rushed to the beach where the boats were kept, stove in six, and put to sea in the seventh. They reached Berbice on Sunday, and Rudio immediately separated from his companions in flight; the rest subsequently came on to this city. The Abeille French wrar steamer, came down from Cayenne in pursuit of fugitives ; and the captain accompanied by the Vice-Consul of France, had an interview with the Governor respecting them. By the extradition Treaty the Governor has no power to deliver up an escaped convict, although he could give up a suspected person. The runaways are at large in the city, and will remain here until they find opportunities of getting away.

BARBADOES. Since writing our last Summary, we have made a recapitulation of the most noticeable features and events of the past year, and have had occasion before to mention the way in which the Christmas season was celebrated, and the opening the New Year. There is but little of to add at present. In fact, nothing has transpired, nor turned up, except a curious coincidence þÿ the washing up out of the Sea on the beach at Fontabelle, a few mornings ago, just after the robbery of the Cathedral Plate, of a silver gilt Goblet, exactly similar in size and shape to those which had been stolen, but not the same, as it wants the device, and bears the evident marks of a long submarine existence. No clue has yet been found to the Sacriligious theft; and it is discovered that leaden Coffins have been removed from the Churchyard surreptitiously. The weather has set in dry and the Canes in consequence tire fast ripening, in many places forced ripe. If there is not a change Sugar-making will be pretty general towards the end of the month. The young plants have sprung well, favored by the recent showers. Yams have been taken in, and have turned out very differently ; in some places remarkably well, in others þÿ we fear in most places þÿ the contrary. We hear it said that the preparations for the young Crop have been made in a superior manner, owing, no doubt to the character of the past year, and the discredit of foreign manures, which has induced Planters to pay more attention to the making up of

home manure, and moulding the land. The following are the salient points of the very important pamphlet by M. de la Guerroniere, which has just been published þÿ of course by permission þÿ at Paris : þÿ We are of the opinion that tlie separation of the Romagna would not tend to diminish the temporal power of the Pope. His territory, it is true, would be diminished, but his political au'hoiity, disencumbered of a resistance which paralysi s it, would not be weakened, but morally strengthened. For, let us repeat it, the authority of the ILad of the Chuich does not lie in tlie ext, lit of a teriilory which he cannot r, tain except by the support ol foreign arms, and in the number of subjects which he is obliged to oppress to make them submit; it lies in the confidence and respect which lie inspires, aud which relieve him from having recourse to extreme measures of tigour and constraint, bad for all Governments, hut especially so lor a Prince who reigns Gospel in hand What matters it, then, to the prestige, to the dignity, to the greatness of the Sovereign Pontiff, tho square miles comprised in his Stales ? Does lie want space to be beloved and venerated ? Are not his benedictions and bis teachings tlie most powerful and not love manifestation of his right ? Does ho bless the whole universe ? Whether he rules over lew or many, that is not the question ; what is essential is that he should have a sufficient number of subjects to be independent, and that lie should not have of too many to bo carried away by those currents passions,
of intorests, of novoltics which arc produced

everywhere where there are considerable agglomerations. The importance of the Pope does not consist in the 21 provinces which he actually possesses. Bologna, Aucona, and Ravenna, separated fiom Rome hy a chain of mountains, the character of their inhabitants and historical souvenirs add nothing to the splendour of Rome. Rome, his seat at the Vatican, is what The Pope throning awes at ( frnppe ) the world. The Sovereign of the Roman States is scarcely thought of.

ther, it would not he restoring to him respectful, submissive and devoted subjects, ready to ! over Maalingen til det Kongelige Gouobey his behests ; it would be giving hitn etie- , mies of his power, resolved to resist him, and whom force alone could keep under. \\ hat would the Church gain thereby ? It would be obliged to see unfaithful sons in rebellious subjects, and to excommunicate those it ought to strike. To assert its sovereignty it would, perhaps, have to reuounee its noblest title þÿ that ot Mother. This is not what it desires. This is not what the Bishops and the Catholics desire. A resumption of possession acquired at such sacrifices would bo a disaster and not a triumph. For 100,000 inhabitants restored to tlie temporal sway of the Pope, it would give a blow to his spiritual authority from which the protectiou of God and the wisdom of Europe will know how to proteot it. But this is not all. Let us take tin impossible supposition that the Church dees not f ar this damage, and that the Pope does not retreat before this extremity ; let us suppose that it is agreed to restore the Romagua to the Pontifical Government, þÿ how is it to he done ? Is it by the voice of persuasion and by good couiimjI i But those means have been exhausted. The Emperor of the French, who has constantly defended the rights of the Holy See, has exercised all his moral authority to calm the public mind in Central Italy, and to reconcile the populations with their former Governments. It has

not succeeded, and its influence failed before the impossible. There remains, then, but one meansþÿ force. It is force only which can restore the Romagna to the condition imposed upon it by treaties and by history. Can it he employed ? And if employed, who is to be it Austria ? charged with executing it ? A liberal nation, she could not compel a people to submit to a Government which their will rejects. Catholics who seek such a triumph for the Church appear to us as dangerous for it as would be for the j Monarchy the Royalists who would dream of re-establishing the ancient legitimacy by the aid of a new invasion. As regards compelling peoples, France is not used to it such she meddled in their affairs was to enfranchise work. They are two hypotheses equally inadmissable, and both, though radically contrary to each other, would have the same result for the Papacy. We believe there is another course that may be taken. First, we wish that the Congress should recognise as an essential principle of European order the necessity of the temporal power of the principle Pope. That is for us the us to chief here appears to have point. The more value than the territorial possession, more or less ex-

tensive, that will be its natural consequences. As for this territory itself, the city of Rome includes all that is most important in it ; the rest is only secondary. The city of Rome and the patrimony of St. Peter must be guaranteed to the Sovereign Pontiff bv the great Powers, with a considerable revenue, that the Catholic States will pay, as a tribute of respect and protection to the Head of the Church. An Italian militia, chosen from the elite of the Federal army, should assure the tranquility and inviolability of the Holy See. Municipal liberties, as extensive as possible, should release the Papal Government from all the details of administration, and thus give a share of public local life to those who are disinherited of political activity.
